questions.question: In hypothesis testing, what does the null hypothesis typically represent?
options: The default position of no effect or no difference, which the test tries to find evidence against.
The result the researcher hopes to prove true.
The probability that the data is correct.
The alternative we accept by default.
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis states no effect or no difference and is assumed true until the data gives strong evidence against it. The alternative is what you suspect instead. A test never proves the null; it either rejects it or fails to reject it.

questions.scenario: A medical screening test's null hypothesis is that a patient is healthy. The test flags a healthy patient as diseased.
questions.question: Which error is this, and what is the other type?
options: A Type 1 error (false positive): rejecting a true null. A Type 2 error is a false negative: failing to reject a false null.
No error; the test did its job.
A sampling error; the other is a rounding error.
A Type 2 error (false negative); the other is a false positive.
questions.explanation: Flagging a healthy patient wrongly rejects a true null, which is a Type 1 error, a false positive. Missing a truly diseased patient would fail to reject a false null, a Type 2 error, a false negative. The significance level controls the Type 1 rate.
questions.misconception: Type 1 is the false positive (reject a true null); Type 2 is the false negative. Keep the direction straight.

questions.scenario: A team runs an A/B test, sees nothing at the planned stop, keeps collecting data, and stops the moment the result crosses significance.
questions.question: Why does this inflate the false-positive rate?
options: It does not; stopping early is always valid.
Repeatedly testing and stopping on significance (peeking) gives the statistic many chances to cross the threshold by chance, so the true Type 1 rate exceeds the stated level.
Collecting more data always reduces false positives, so this is fine.
The problem is only that the sample is too large.
questions.explanation: A fixed significance level assumes one test at a predetermined sample size. Peeking and stopping when it crosses the line means many implicit tests, each a fresh chance to cross by random noise, so the real false-positive rate climbs well above the nominal level. Fixed-horizon designs or sequential-testing corrections avoid this.
questions.misconception: More data is not a free pass. Optional stopping on significance breaks the Type 1 guarantee.
